title: Why robot embodiment matters: questions of disability, race and intersectionality in the design of social robots

# Why robot embodiment matters: questions of disability, race and intersectionality in the design of social robots

PMC11877043. Medical Humanities, 50(4):e013028. Published 2024-10-28.

## Authors

Mark Paterson

## Details

- DOI: https://doi.org/10.1136/medhum-2024-013028
- PMID: 39467645 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39467645/)
- PMCID: PMC11877043
- License: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/

---

## Abstract

A growing minority of those with disabilities are people of color (POC), with, for example, autism diagnosis rates now higher for children of color than for white children in the USA. This trend underscores the need for assistive technologies, especially socially assistive robots, to be designed with intersectional users in mind. Outside of Japan, most robots are designed with white synthetic skin and able-bodied features, failing to reflect the diverse users they are meant to assist. This paper explores the concept of the "engineering imaginary," the historical and cultural influences that shape these designs, and which tend to limit robot embodiment to white, able-bodied forms. Drawing on work from scholars like Lucy Suchman, Jennifer Rhee, Neda Atanasoski and Kalindi Vora, the paper critiques this engineering bias. A key historical moment in the production of the engineered imaginary of artificial humans is provided by Ovid’s myth of Pygmalion and its influence on representations across literature, film, and then robotics. Furthermore, the physicality of the robot, and its role in the production of nonverbal communication (NVC) for more inclusive interaction with humans is explored, seeing these as steps toward what some roboticists are calling Artificial Empathy (AE). Through case studies like Bestic, Bina48, and HuggieBot 3.0, the paper explores what I call the poverty of the engineering imaginary, how current robotics design fails to properly address issues of race, gender, and disability. Ultimately, the paper argues for more inclusive robot designs that accommodate diverse bodies and social dynamics, questioning the pervasive norm of white, able-bodied robotic embodiment.

The global market for assistive technologies is expanding rapidly, and these technologies include robotics. Of those with disabilities, an increasingly visible and growing minority are people of colour (POC). According to a report on autism by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in the USA, rates of diagnoses for autism in children of colour is now higher than for their white counterparts (CDC 2023). Clearly, those robots tasked with social interaction (social robots), and especially robots tasked with assistive roles (socially assistive robots), need to be designed and engineered with multiple forms of difference in mind. In other words, the global market of assistive technologies must acknowledge that a growing intersectional population will be using their products, and of those assistive technologies, robots will have to be designed to interact with this intersectional population. The problem, as it stands, is that few robots look anything like the users they will interact with. Furthermore, this reveals a more fundamental issue in the design of robot morphologies: outside of Japan, which has its own rather culturally specific relationship to race and representation in robots, the vast majority of robot platforms available in the Global North involve white plastic or even Caucasian synthetic skin, and insofar as the design intention was to appear humanoid, their morphology is able-bodied, even if their actual abilities are variable. How did it come to be like this? One answer pursued in this paper is what I call the poverty of the ‘engineering imaginary’.

As part of my ongoing research on the role of robot morphology and interaction design for human-robot interactions (HRIs) (eg, Paterson 2023; Zheng, Lacey, and Paterson 2020; Paterson, Hoffman, and Zheng 2023; Zheng et al 2024), in this paper I specifically address the question of the engineered imaginaries behind humanoid robot embodiment, and why they predominantly instantiate white and able bodies. It furthers a rather controversial story in The Conversation on the ‘whiteness’ of robots (Paterson 2024b). To this end, it is conceptually aided by the work of Lucy Suchman, the anthropologist of science and technology, who writes about cultural imaginaries and material figurations in her Human-Machine Reconfigurations (2007). In later chapters, Suchman attempts to combine the situated empirical observation of interactions with machines with what she calls ‘an interest in cultural historical continuities and their effects’ (2007, 16). These two intertwining strands, the empirical and the cultural-historical, I consider as particularly pertinent in studying the prevailing trends in robot morphology and interaction design, and can be generative of research prompts for critiquing the ‘engineering imaginary’. Consequently, in the second section I argue that the design and engineering of robot morphologies, and therefore robot embodiment, matters, as the culmination of a series of intentional design choices which produce or negate affordances for users within HRIs. From Lucy Suchman, then, and related work on robot imaginaries by Rhee (2018), and further explorations of the ‘engineered imaginary’ by Atanasoski and Vora (2019), the concept of the ‘engineered imaginary’ is defined and advanced here, the idea that current design practices are limited by historical imaginaries that keep humanoid robots white and predominantly female. In the third section, ‘Ovid’s legacy’, I offer some cultural and literary historical perspectives to begin to address the question of the formation of that historical imaginary, at least in the Graeco-Roman context, as a foundation for literary, poetic and later filmic imaginaries of artificial humans. There is no single foundational myth, nor any particular paradigmatic representation of humanoid robot morphology. However, the Roman poet Ovid’s recounting of the myth of the sculptor Pygmalion and his marble creation Galatea, and subsequent reimaginings and reinterpretations of that myth in literature and film, point to consistent (and persistent) confluences of raced and gendered morphologies across different time periods, rendered within different media. Ideas often raised here in narratives of seduction through mimicry are echoed in the fourth section, on the topic of ‘Artificial empathy’ (AE). Although artificial intelligence (AI) is a topic of intense interest right now, the manifestation of AE is an aim for roboticists like Minoru Asada in some papers (Asada 2015a; Asada 2015b), and a recent book Living With Robots by Paul Dumouchel and Luisa Damiano (2017), where physical embodiment, movement and non-verbal communicative gestures all play a part in its production (Dumouchel and Damiano 2017). The example of an encounter between Sherry Turkle and her fellow MIT robot Kismet is used as a departure point to consider the role of certain forms of physicality and mimicry in the production of an illusion of connection between non-human robot and human user. The paper concludes with some general thoughts about the role of embodiment and the need to imagine otherwise.

A wide range of robot examples is provided throughout, but it should be clarified that the design of robot bodies and their gestural and vocal capacities is only part of the story. In each section, a key example of a social or service robot, and reflections on their physicality, are given. For each key example I stress their different contexts and users, and how they involve different social dynamics. There is a significant difference between a complex assistive robot in a hospital or assisted care setting, for example, which must be operated and maintained by skilled staff, and the inexpensive toys such as Hasbro’s ‘Joy For All’ robotic companion animals available to consumers. In other words, the materiality of robotics extends beyond the robot design and their platforms and into these social settings. Three examples in particular help us understand robotics design responses, and therefore the ‘engineered imaginary’, to the social categories raised earlier of gender, race and disability. The first example is Bestic, a rather specialised feeding assistant robot arm from Sweden that is very minimally embodied. The second is based on a series of video art installations by African-American artist Stephanie Dinkins of Bina48, one of the only instances of the robotic embodiment of an African-American person, modelled on the head and shoulders of the chief engineer’s wife. The third is HuggieBot 3.0 from Alexis E. Block at the Max Planck Institute in Stuttgart and now the Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, a larger-than-human robot with padded torso and articulated arms designed to employ social touch to human volunteers in close proximity. From these, and a number of other brief examples, we can extrapolate and ask: how are interaction designers conceiving of more accessible interactions for those with visible and non-visible disabilities, and taking account of racial and gender differences? Why is the ‘norm’ for robot embodiment so pervasively white and able-bodied, and how might considerations of bodily difference be incorporated into future robot design? Ultimately, how can HRI be made more inclusive for literally every body?

## The rise of disability robotics

First, consider the sheer market opportunities for those with disabilities around the world. From large multinational consumer technology companies to tiny robotics startups, innovations are specifically targeting users with disabilities. According to a WHO factsheet on disability, 1.3 billion people, amounting to about 16% of the global population, currently experience significant disability (WHO 2023). This number will increase due in part to population ageing, as well as an increase in the prevalence of non-communicable diseases. Meanwhile, in a 2021 World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) report, it is estimated that 1 billion people require assistive technology globally, and that ‘this figure is expected to reach 2 billion by 2050 as the population ages and consumer electronics and assistive products converge’ (WIPO 2021, 14). Innovations in robotics and computing have increasingly been directed to the area of human-machine interaction, where communication between human and technoscientific object involves multiple faculties and sensory modalities, including speech, hearing, vision and motor abilities. According to the WIPO report, ‘special software and services for assistive communication technologies had the highest number of patent filings between 1998 and 2019, especially in the area of emulation software which transforms the user interface of a device (including hardware input devices) into a customised software interface for easier interaction and accessibility for users’, writes Yokoi (2022). Furthermore, tech companies in the consumer space including Apple, Samsung, Microsoft and Sony are addressing such user interaction and accessibility issues in software and operating systems, but also hardware including videogame controllers such as the Adaptive Controller from Microsoft, able to be reconfigured according to a user’s differing motor capacities. Robots, and more particularly social robots designed for assisted living, have been poised to enter this space for quite some time, but significant shortcomings in HRIs must be addressed first. While having a mobile device in one’s hand with an accessible user interface is one thing, approaching and interacting with a humanoid robot is a less inviting, and potentially more off-putting, prospect (e.g. Paterson 2023).
